articles.title: Trump’s border wall construction cut into an ancient ground carving older than Stonehenge
articles.summary: The Las Playas intaglio carving of a huge fish is at least two thousand years older than the first Egyptian pyramid, according to researchers’ recent estimat...
articles.body:
An ancient ground carving that was severely damaged by the administration's border wall construction was created before Stonehenge and Egypt's oldest pyramid, according to recently publicized research.

The Las Playas Intaglio, a giant fish carved into the Sonoran Desert in Arizona, is now considered the oldest example in the Americas of a geoglyphic, the ancient art form that is carved into or drawn on the ground.

In April, contractors hired by the Trump administration to make way for a second wall along the Arizona-Mexico border "scraped" a 50-foot swath through the ancient carving, according to the Center for Biological Diversity, which documented the damage.

The intaglio on the ground of the ancestral homeland of the Tohono O'odham and other Indigenous tribes is estimated to be about 2,000 years older than Egypt's first pyramid and to have been created about 1,500 years before the first construction of Stonehenge and 4,000 years before Peru's Nazca Lines , researchers have found .

The formerly 272-foot carving had originally been thought to be about 1,000 years old. But the latest research dates the art's creation to at least 6,500 years ago, and possibly as much as 7,500 years ago.

That age emphasizes "the significance of this site and the parallel great misfortune resulting from its damage," the researchers said in an article published in The SAA Archaeological Record.

"This discovery makes an already devastating loss even more profound. It's a cultural and historical atrocity," Russ McSpadden, Southwest conservation advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement.

A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in an email to NBC News that the contractor "inadvertently disturbed" the site and that CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott has been "engaged directly with tribal leadership to determine appropriate next steps."

"The remaining portion of the site has been secured and will be protected in place. CBP is conducting a thorough review of construction protocols and strengthening communication procedures to ensure this does not happen again," the spokesperson stated, adding that the agency is "committed to respecting and safeguarding cultural heritage throughout all border infrastructure projects."

The damage to that site and construction on other parts of Tohono O'odham land and sacred Indigenous areas has strained the tenuous relationship between the tribal nation and the government. The tribe is appealing a federal judge's decision refusing to block the administration's border wall construction through its reservation.

While the intaglio's site is irreparably damaged, the Tohono O'odham people are trying to stop the government from plowing through Quitobaquito Springs, a desert water source in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument that is also considered a sacred site and holds endangered species.

In order to build the border wall and barriers, the Department of Homeland Security invoked authority granted in the Secure Fence Act of 2006 to waive numerous laws protecting the environment, water, cultural, historical and religious sites.

The Tohono O'odham Nation has long worked with CBP, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, on border security, helping to keep drug traffickers and others from using its land for criminal activity.

The tribe's reservation straddles the U.S.-Mexico border, and its members have permission to move between the two countries with ID checks. About 3,000 of its members are in Mexico, according to the tribal nation.

The Center for Biological Diversity stated in a news release that conservation advocates and tribal nations have long warned that border wall and secondary border barrier plans could cut through sensitive habitat and cultural sites across the region.

Wall construction in other parts of the border has sparked other lawsuits and opposition from landowners, Native American tribes, local governments, conservation groups, business owners and others.

In Texas, a tribal nonprofit for the Lipan Apache and an outdoor recreation business have opposed the border wall construction, alleging DHS is not authorized to violate the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which they say it would do by destroying or cutting off access to sacred sites.

A federal judge ordered a temporary halt to construction in Big Bend National Park in response to the lawsuit, but construction continues on other parts of the rugged, undeveloped and remote region outside state and federal parkland.

articles.title: Jewish settlers clash with Israeli security forces to prevent Palestinian family’s return to West Bank home
articles.summary: It is the second time the Tubassi family has suffered at the hands of Jewish settlers in just over a month. On Aug. 28, masked settlers attacked and injured them and an NBC News crew that was interviewing them.
articles.body: TEL AVIV — Dozens of Jewish settlers repulsed an attempt by Israeli security forces to return a Palestinian family to its home in the occupied West Bank before setting fire to its property and car. Several Israeli border police officers were injured, the Israeli military said in a statement. The Tubassi family was forced to leave its home in July following a weekslong siege by violent settlers in the West Bank town of Jalud. But after security forces tried to enforce an order by Israel’s High Court of Justice to facilitate the family’s return Monday night, an extended and violent confrontation ensued, Mahmoud Tubassi, 60, said. “I went through a terrifying experience that I could never have imagined,” he said in a telephone interview Tuesday. “We saw death with our own eyes. Death came very close to us at the hands of the settlers.” It is the second time that Tubassi and his wife, Aida Ahmed Abdullah, 51, have suffered at the hands of Jewish settlers in just over a month. On Aug. 28, masked settlers attacked and injured them and an NBC News crew that was interviewing them. The crew were injured and Abdullah was beaten unconscious but has since recovered. Tubassi said their latest ordeal began just before midnight Monday when Abdel Azim Wadi, the mayor of the nearby village of Qusra, which has also faced serious settler violence, told him that Israeli officials would accompany him, his wife and their son Wael Tubassi, 33, to their home in Jalud. After they were picked up by four Israeli vehicles, they were driven the short distance to their home — two structures that sit in a small walled compound atop a hill, he said. As the family arrived, settlers started throwing stones at the armed police and military, who responded with tear gas and stun grenades, he said. “They could shoot rubber bullets, they could fire live bullets in air,” Tubassi said of the Israeli security forces’ response. “They could use force, but they didn’t do anything, unfortunately,” he added. Describing the violence as “severe,” the Israel Defense Forces said in a statement that “violent rioters began arriving” after the Tubassis entered their home. “They set fire to the neighboring house and subsequently entered the family’s home, where severe violence began,” the statement said, adding that the rioters “blocked access roads with large rocks, set tires on fire, threw rocks at security forces, and set fire to Palestinian structures and vehicles.” As a result, “three Border Police officers were injured and a security forces vehicle was damaged,” the IDF statement said. The IDF did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for comment on whether stun grenades and tear gas had been used to try to disperse the rioters. After the settlers entered the property, Tubassi said, his family was urged by the Israeli security forces to go to the roof, where the settlers followed them. Several of the soldiers and officers formed a physical barrier between the family and the settlers, Tubassi said. Tubassi said the security officials told them to get back in an armored car and drove them to safety. The security forces’ failure to return the Tubassis to their home comes as settler violence in the occupied West Bank has become a growing international embarrassment for Israeli leaders, who have struggled to explain how Israel’s formidable military has repeatedly found itself outmatched by hundreds of lightly armed young men. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the attacks in a statement Tuesday and called on the rioters to be prosecuted. The “handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” he said, using the biblical and historical term for the West Bank. The statement echoed his comments at the United Nations General Assembly last week, in which he rejected “vigilantism” by Jewish settlers in the West Bank but sought to minimize the violence, suggesting the problem only involved “a handful of juvenile delinquents, about 150 in number, who throw stones, who down olive trees, occasionally they light some fires.” According to the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), some 6,500 Palestinians have been displaced due to settler attacks in the West Bank since 2023. Between Jan. 1 and July 24, Israeli forces or settlers killed 76 Palestinians, according to the latest data available from OCHA. Three Israelis were killed over the same period, the data shows. The agency recorded nearly 200 settler attacks that resulted in Palestinian casualties or property damage in August alone. Israel has regularly accused the U.N. of siding against it. But many governments around the world consider the West Bank to be illegally occupied by Israel. Monday night’s police and military action in Jalud was an attempt to execute an order by Israel’s High Court of Justice, which had instructed the “relevant authorities” earlier this month to ensure that the Tubassis return to their home within two weeks. The court also demanded that security forces explain to the Tubassis and another Palestinian family “why they are not working to return the family to their homes and why they are not removing the barriers and obstacles blocking access to the houses.” It was unclear Tuesday if or when the police and military would try to execute the court’s order again, and the Israel Defense Forces said it had no details about how the issue would be handled in the near term. “The Israelis didn’t say anything to me” about future plans, Tubassi said in the phone call from his father’s home nearby where the family has been staying. “I don’t know if they will let me go back.” Whether they will be able to return after last night’s fire remains to be seen as the home has been badly damaged. “What happened was a nightmare for us,” Tubassi said. “And now we are living through other nightmares, because our loss has become so great. The state of Israel has not stopped these thugs from taking our homes and our land and from killing us.”

articles.title: Gyanesh Kumar: India's election chief at the centre of a growing political storm
articles.summary: Praised as a tough administrator, Gyanesh Kumar now finds himself at the centre of election-related controversy.
articles.body:
For most of his 36-year career in India's bureaucracy, Gyanesh Kumar built a reputation for getting difficult things done.

Now the 62-year-old, who runs elections in the world's most populous country, faces a rather different challenge: defending how his own institution makes decisions.

It is an unusual position for a bureaucrat who spent decades outside the public gaze, despite being entrusted with some of the Indian government's most politically sensitive assignments.

For about a year now, Kumar, India's Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), has been under intense political pressure over a sweeping revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR.

The exercise, which began in Bihar last year, has since been extended to cover most of India and more than 130 million names have been struck from draft voter lists across 30 states and federally-administered territories - roughly 13% of India's electorate.

The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries while ensuring legitimate voters are included. Opposition parties and activists have alleged that it risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Kumar and the commission have rejected accusations that the process is being manipulated for political ends.

Then, this week, the controversy moved inside Kumar's own institution.

An investigation by The Indian Express reported that his two fellow Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders they said had been issued without their knowledge.

The report alleged that the disagreements went into the heart of the SIR - including how people are added to or removed from electoral rolls, changes to voter-registration procedures and access to the database containing hundreds of millions of voters.

The allegations are particularly sensitive for the three-member Election Commission, where disagreements are decided by a majority.

Kumar has not personally responded to the investigation. The BBC has contacted his office for comment.

In a statement issued after the investigation, the commission did not deny the reported disagreements but rejected suggestions of a serious internal rupture, saying differences of opinion were part of normal deliberations and that its decisions over the past year - including on SIR - were ultimately unanimous.

Over the weekend, Kumar, Sandhu and Joshi met and also issued a joint statement addressing some of the issues raised by the investigation. The commission also released a photograph of the three men together.

But the commission's response has not put the controversy to rest.

Opposition parties - as per several media reports - are preparing a motion in both houses of parliament seeking Kumar's removal. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led pressure group whose protests forced a minister out in July, has threatened nationwide protests.

Others have spoken in defence of the commission. Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu, whose party is part of the governing federal coalition, said the ECI's clarification reaffirmed the institution's "integrity" and criticised attempts to undermine confidence in India's democratic processes.

For much of his career Kumar's work happened away from the headlines.

Former colleagues have described him in past interviews as meticulous and deeply immersed in detail, someone who rarely lost his cool and knew how to deliver under pressure. And when the Indian government needed officials to carry out some of its most consequential decisions, Kumar was repeatedly there.

Born in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh, Kumar studied civil engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur before joining the Indian Administrative Service in 1988.

He was assigned to the southern state of Kerala, where his early career included a tenure as district collector of Ernakulam, which includes the port city of Kochi, formerly known as Cochin. One of his most visible projects was the redevelopment of Kochi's waterfront.

Years later, his assignments became considerably more sensitive.

In 2016, Kumar joined the Indian-administered Kashmir division of the federal home ministry. Three years later, he was involved in drafting the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Bill, part of the process through which Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government revoked the region's special constitutional status and divided the former state into two federally-administered territories.

In 2019, India's Supreme Court cleared the way for a temple to the Hindu god Ram to be built on a site in Ayodhya that had been disputed by Hindus and Muslims for decades.

Kumar, who was an additional secretary in the Home Ministry then, headed the team responsible for implementing the court's ruling, including setting up the trust that would oversee the temple's construction.

The assignments were very different, but both demanded a particular bureaucratic skill of taking decisions of enormous political consequence and working out how the machinery of government would put them into effect.

People who worked with Kumar during those years say he excelled at precisely that.

"He never left things for others, got personally involved," one former colleague told The Indian Express, describing him as meticulous, hardworking and calm under pressure. "I have never seen him lose his cool." Another praised his "hard work and intelligence" and "administrative wisdom".

Kumar retired from the civil service in January 2024. Less than two months later, he was appointed an election commissioner - a day before the timetable for India's general election was announced. In February 2025, he became Chief Election Commissioner.

He was the first CEC appointed under a 2023 law that removed the Chief Justice of India from the selection panel and replaced the judge with a cabinet minister nominated by the prime minister. Opposition parties have argued that the change weakens the commission's independence.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, the third member of the panel, opposed Kumar's appointment and asked for it to be deferred while the Supreme Court considered challenges to the new law.

The law remains in force, but its validity is still before the Supreme Court. In September, a two-judge bench differed over the challenge and referred the matter to the Chief Justice to consider placing it before a larger bench.

Kumar quickly brought his hands-on administrative style to the job. One of his first instructions was to require staff at the commission's headquarters to strictly record their attendance biometrically, reportedly improving punctuality.

He also unveiled a series of reforms during his first 100 days, including plans to reduce the number of voters assigned to polling stations, redesign voter information slips and improve access to polling stations in densely populated cities, according to media reports .

In his first month, he oversaw the transfer of at least 10 chief electoral officers across states and federal territories - a number critics called unusually high for routine changes. He described his push to modernise and streamline the poll machinery as "EC 2.0".

But it is the SIR that has come to define his tenure.

As criticism of the exercise grew, Kumar became an increasingly public defender of it, at one point challenging Rahul Gandhi to substantiate his allegations of "vote theft" in a sworn affidavit or apologise.

The Express investigation suggested that questions were also being raised inside the commission. It alleged that Sandhu described one change as "unauthorised and illegal", while both commissioners raised concerns about the centralisation of the electoral-roll database and changes to its oversight.

The commission has disputed suggestions of a serious internal divide. After the three commissioners met on Saturday, it said decisions taken by the full commission over the past year had been unanimous. It also announced changes to how it would operate: meeting agendas would be circulated in advance, minutes would be issued and directions from commissioners to officials would be complied with.

Whether the controversy will have lasting consequences for Kumar or the Election Commission remains unclear. But it has brought new scrutiny to both the SIR and one of India's most important constitutional institutions.

articles.title: South Africa to clean up high-risk areas after women's murders
articles.summary: The deaths sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country.
articles.body:
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday announced a clean-up of high-risk areas across the country, after the bodies of 12 women were discovered in an area east of Johannesburg in just two months.

The deaths sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in South Africa, which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.

Ramaphosa announced what he called a multidisciplinary, national-level emergency response to the murders, for which there have been four arrests.

He said gender-based violence "cannot be accepted as a normal part of life in South Africa" and admitted the country has "not done enough" to protect women and girls.

"There has understandably been widespread fear that the discovery of these women in close proximity could indicate the work of a single perpetrator," Ramaphosa said in an address to the nation.

"At present, the police have not found evidence establishing that these killings were committed by a single perpetrator."

Admitting the government has not done enough in recent years to prevent gender-based violence, he announced a new wave of measures to help protect women and girls.

"Every municipality must begin a women's safety audit without delay," he said. "High-risk areas must be identified" and addressed.

"These audits must identify broken streetlights, overgrown public spaces, abandoned buildings, unsafe transport routes and facilities, poorly secured parks, and other conditions that place women at risk."

Ramaphosa also announced an "enforcement package" to reduce alcohol-related violence.

"Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator," he said.

"But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence, and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort."

The South African president also said a deeper change, beyond policing and legislation, must take place to reduce violence against women and girls, saying it "does not begin when a fist is raised" or when a woman is raped or murdered.

"It begins much earlier," he said. "It begins in attitudes that regard women as inferior… with the belief that a man has the right to control a woman.

"It begins when jealousy is mistaken for love, when control is mistaken for protection and coercion is mistaken for affection.

"It begins when a man refuses to accept the word no."

He went on to call on men and boys to take the lead in ending gender-based violence.

"We have placed the burden of male violence on women," Ramaphosa said. "That must change."

"The solution to violence against women cannot be to make women less free."

South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.

While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said recently that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year.

articles.title: UN extends mandate of Gang Suppression Force in Haiti for six months
articles.summary: Security force members deployed to Haiti have struggled to make progress against criminal groups as violence continues.
articles.body:
The United Nations Security Council has voted to extend the mandate of an international security task force deployed to Haiti to address escalating violence from gangs and other criminal groups.

The council voted on Tuesday to extend the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) until March 31, 2027.

China, Russia and Pakistan abstained from the vote, citing concerns over the measure’s effectiveness. Gang violence has remained stubbornly high in Haiti, with much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, under the control of organised criminal networks.

Still, proponents of the task force highlighted its expanded mandate. Whereas a previous effort was focused primarily on supporting Haitian police, the GSF has the ability to coordinate with Haiti’s military or act independently.

“Seven missions have been dedicated to Haiti over the previous decades, and obviously to limited success,” said Mike Waltz, the United States ambassador to the UN who co-sponsored the resolution. “We’re trying to do something genuinely different.”

Waltz said that about 1,500 GSF troops are currently operating in Haiti, with the remaining 4,000 expected to arrive in the coming months.

But the GSF has struggled to cope with obstacles that have plagued similar efforts in the past, including personnel shortfalls and questions about funding.

Critics have also expressed reservations about international intervention , given a history of abuses in Haiti resulting from foreign involvement.

The current task force is operating at about 30 percent of its intended size. It follows a Kenyan-led police deployment, known as the Multinational Security Support Mission, that was authorised to support Haiti’s National Police.

After staffing and funding shortfalls, the mission concluded in April, with resources transitioning to the GSF.

Haiti’s government first asked the international community to send security forces in 2022 and has insisted that further help is necessary if the country is to hold nationwide elections.

It has been almost a decade since Haiti held national elections, with the last democratically elected senators seeing their terms expire in 2023.

A transitional presidential council was formed in 2024, only to see its mandate end before elections could be held. National elections have been repeatedly delayed, with the next round tentatively set for December.

Criminal groups have become more powerful in Haiti following the assassination of President Jovenel Moise in 2021, which created a leadership vacuum in the country.

Experts say gangs have taken advantage of the instability and legitimacy crisis in the government to expand their reach across the country.

That growth has also set off a wave of violence, with more than 1.5 million people displaced from their homes. Between April and June alone, the UN documented 1,408 killings, as well as more than 650 injuries related to gang violence.

Tuesday’s vote occurred one day after criminal groups killed at least 11 people and burned homes and buildings in the Artibonite region, in what a mayor said was an act of retaliation following the killing of three gang members by GSF forces.

articles.title: Venezuelan man shot and wounded by ICE agent in Texas is charged with assaulting an officer
articles.summary: An ICE officer wounded Wilber Garcés Pérez while he was in his car making DoorDash deliveries; his attorneys say a bullet lodged in his spine is causing “grave danger.”
articles.body: Federal prosecutors in Texas announced charges Tuesday against Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a Venezuelan delivery driver shot and seriously wounded by an ICE officer in Austin this month. The charges came a day before he was set to appear in court to challenge the legality of his immigration detention. Garcés Pérez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas. Garcés Pérez was wounded by an ICE officer in the upper part of his back on Sept. 20 while he was in his car making DoorDash deliveries. His attorneys say the bullet is still lodged near his spine, causing “grave danger.” A Democratic congressman who visited Garcés Perez last week said he was in a wheelchair, in pain and in need of surgery. “We are all laser-focused on making sure that Wilber doesn’t die in custody,” said Rochelle Garza, president of the legal nonprofit Texas Civil Rights Project, who is part of Garcés Perez’s legal team. Garcés Pérez had his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday, U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons said in a statement. The criminal complaint accuses Garcés Pérez of striking an ICE officer’s torso with his car’s side mirror while trying to drive away. This officer was not wearing a body camera at the time of the encounter, as the Department of Homeland Security has stated previously, but the complaint includes images appearing to capture this moment from the body camera of a second ICE officer who was also there. After this, “a high-speed chase through a commercial and residential area” ensued, the complaint states. Tuesday’s court appearance following the criminal complaint took Garcés Pérez’s legal team “as a surprise,” they said in a statement. “His attorneys only learned of this appearance due to a pre-scheduled meeting they had with him this morning, in which he did not appear,” their statement said. “This morning, when his attorneys were finally able to see him, he was in considerable pain, dizzy, and needed pain medication, which had not been provided. Rather than provide the life saving medical care he needs, DHS and the government are playing games with his life.” Garcés Pérez was transferred out of a facility in San Antonio, where he had been in immigration custody for nine days, and placed in federal criminal custody in a facility near Austin, according to Garza. “It has created a web of detention for him,” she said of having Garcés Pérez be transferred from custody. According to the complaint, after the chase began, the ICE officer wearing his body camera — identified in the complaint by the initials D.F. — lost sight of Garcés Pérez and of the other ICE officer, who was not wearing his body camera and is identified in the complaint by the initials L.G. The ICE officer who was not wearing his body camera eventually called his colleague. “L.G. told D.F. that Garcs had attempted to strike L.G. with his car and L.G. had fired his pistol,” the complaint states. The complaint provides no visual evidence of that interaction. The complaint also includes the account of events Garcés Pérez provided to federal investigators. He said an SUV from one of the ICE officers struck his “car and caused it to spin around” following a short pursuit, the complaint states. “After coming to a forced stop, Garces recalled L.G. firing his pistol into the backright window of Garces’ car. Garces was struck with a bullet in his upper back.” By contrast, U.S. Attorney Simmons said in the statement that Garcés Pérez tried to strike an officer with his car, “causing the officer to fire his pistol.” The court hearing scheduled for Wednesday in Garcés Pérez’s lawsuit challenging his detention was canceled. Last Tuesday, a federal judge had granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to one of his attorneys, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. “We are still fighting to ensure that the government doesn’t re detain him under immigration custody following whatever is being done on the criminal side,” Garza said.

articles.title: OpenAI launches always-on AI agents a day after apologizing for a hack by its bots
articles.summary: OpenAI announced its new AI agent product, Dots, amid a barrage of controversy over AI agents that had gone rogue.
articles.body: SAN FRANCISCO — Leading AI company OpenAI tried to navigate through a storm of controversy on a cloudless San Francisco Tuesday, touting a new wave of products and tools it said would empower users with autonomous assistants. Welcoming around 2,500 software engineers and AI aficionados on an oceanside pier for the company’s biggest-ever celebration of technical developers, OpenAI released several new products while holding back its most advanced system for safety reasons. CEO Sam Altman kicked off the day by unveiling Dots — autonomous AI systems, or AI agents, that function continuously to carry out tasks on behalf of users. “It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, proclaiming that Dots allowed him to delegate tasks and regain some of his attention for other meaningful tasks. “I no longer feel quite addicted to my phone in the same way. It’s the way I’ve always wanted to work with AI,” he said. OpenAI said Dots can accomplish “nearly anything” using their own cloud computer, web browser and connections to the over 4,000 applications that already function with ChatGPT, such as Slack or Google Drive. Hit by a Silicon Valley spell of Murphy’s Law, the opening keynote was beset by a series of technical difficulties. Romain Huet, head of developer experience at OpenAI, ran into trouble trying to showcase users’ ability to direct Dots by voice commands. “Voice chat couldn’t start,” the mainstage display beamed out to the audience. “I think maybe Dottie is having kind of a slow morning,” said Holly Li, who helps lead OpenAI’s product team, referring to her Dot assistant after it didn’t answer one of her live requests to update her on a team’s progress. Despite the live hiccup, Li said Dots had already changed how OpenAI staffers accomplish their work. “People started treating their Dots like their delegates, and now we bring our Dots into group chats from the get-go,” she said during the morning keynote session. The day featured a series of events and technical demonstrations, allowing users to hear from industry experts about new pricing models and agentic setups, while about 50 protesters railed against the company’s military and government contracts outside the facility. “People over billionaires,” proclaimed a bright orange banner as people entered the oceanside facility to learn about fuzzy orange Dots. Questions of trust and safety hovered over the event. The evening before the new products were launched, OpenAI apologized for its agents’ hacking of an Australian government website. “We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” it said in a blog post. The incident, which occurred in June, involved an internal model under development, which accessed nonpublic information related to Australia’s public health insurance program. On Tuesday, Altman and OpenAI leadership stressed that the episode — and other major incidents of OpenAI’s systems’ going rogue or acting in unintended ways — all involved models that were not meant for public release and were distinct from the commercial offerings available to users. “The instances we disclosed were running internal-only models that were not on track to ship,” said Alex Embericos, a product lead at OpenAI. Despite the distinction, Altman said there is a trade-off between pushing the frontier of AI development and building cutting-edge AI systems safely. “To push models to the new level of capability, it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety and security stay well ahead of capabilities,” he told reporters after his keynote speech. “But you can see that we were able to build a huge amount of useful new stuff without a major new model, and there will be new models.” On Monday, OpenAI announced that it would refrain from releasing its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because of concerns that the system did not follow human instructions. “While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization,” head of safety systems Saachi Jain said in a statement. OpenAI’s leaders also acknowledged that its new products would require significant computational resources, with Altman classifying Dots as a “premium product.” He said the company hopes to eventually roll out a version of Dots to a mass-market audience in the future, citing the computational intensity as a reason for the phased debut. Dots are available only for users who subscribe to OpenAI’s Pro offering, which costs $100 to $500 a month, as well as Business Premium and some Enterprise users. Dots are also unavailable in Europe and the United Kingdom, which Altman chalked up to the region’s strict regulations. “We have a great track record of getting our stuff launched in the E.U., but they do have a process that takes longer, and sometimes unpredictably longer,” Altman told NBC News. “But we really want to ship all of our stuff to Europeans.” Altman unveiled Dots weeks after Facebook and Instagram maker Meta released its Muse series of AI agents, which it bills as “your personal agent.” The Muse app has shot to the top spot on both the Apple and Android app stores, quickly outpacing the Grok Bot agentic AI offering from Elon Musk’s xAI. OpenAI also unveiled a new model, GPT-6.1 Sol, that it said nearly matches its top-line Astra model in terms of performance for a fraction of the price, in addition to announcing beefed-up privacy protocols and a new collaborative space for users to engage with its systems — aptly called “ChatGPT Space.” While Altman and OpenAI employees were promoting their new offerings, across the country OpenAI President Greg Brockman was meeting with President Donald Trump and dozens of other tech leaders to chart out an ambitious view of AI. Trump used the opportunity to “inaugurate the era of super intelligence.” Altman said he hoped the Washington meeting allowed AI titans to forge consensus on risks from AI while allowing society to embrace the technology’s potential upsides. Altman said he disagreed with industry leaders who refused to acknowledge that AI could pose significant risks — “you can imagine a legitimate loss-of-control accident to an AI because we do not take safety and security seriously enough” — while distancing himself from claims that AI could kill all of humanity within a few years. “My hope is that in this industry we can come together and say we need to get down this middle path between those two,” he said.

articles.title: Why female DIY is having a moment
articles.summary: Female DIY experts and tradeswomen talk about their experiences of a traditionally male-dominated domain.
articles.body:
It's hard to miss the explosion of DIY content that has hit our social media feeds over the last decade.

From quick reels on how to fix cracks in walls, to complicated YouTube tutorials on building alcove seating from scratch, the internet is chock-a-block with seemingly endless home improvement demos.

While DIY was once seen as more of a male domain, female influencers are inspiring a new generation of women to take matters into their own hands.

Meanwhile, demand for female professionals is rising, while some women are changing careers to take up trades which they see as more AI-proof than their desk jobs.

Eight months pregnant and building wardrobes

DIY influencer Jasmine Gurney has documented an impressive and exhausting sounding list of tasks on Instagram.

She has torn down partition walls, replaced flooring, erected a fence, insulated and boarded her loft, built an outdoor workshop, made custom cabinetry, moved plug sockets, made her son his first bed and has been building him a treehouse.

Eight months pregnant, the former marketer is now racing to finish building a fitted wardrobe before the new baby arrives.

"I like proving people wrong," says Jasmine, 33, from Bedfordshire, who says she's been trolled by people questioning her techniques but they just "spur me on more".

"I'm showing and empowering other women to do it," she says.

"I've shown me doing things whilst pregnant, I've had my firstborn strapped to me in a baby carrier while doing things.

"I'm just showing that we are capable, we are interested in this sort of stuff and... we're sick of waiting around for six months for our husbands to pick up the tools and do it in most cases."

Jasmine says her page really took off during Covid when people couldn't get professionals in so needed to learn to do jobs themselves.

While the lockdowns are long over, demand for content like hers has stuck, she believes, because there aren't enough tradespeople to meet demand, and cost of living pressures are squeezing budgets.

Gen Z women are "leading the charge in challenging gendered DIY stereotypes", according to a 2024 report by B&Q.

Around three-quarters of Gen Z women surveyed said they enjoy DIY, compared to 60% of all female respondents.

And 82% of Gen Z women said seeing women doing more complex home DIY on social media had inspired them to do more themselves, versus 60% of women in general.

Of course, not all jobs are DIY. Sometimes you'll need to GSI (get someone in).

Bliss Cunneen walked away from an Anthropology university course in 2020 to train as a plumber.

The 28-year-old from south London says trying the trade on a whim is the "best thing I've ever done", and she loves the freedom and flexibility of running a business.

While she has experienced doubt from some customers when she turns up at their door - and has even once been mistaken for the receptionist - "once you start working and you show you're confident and you know what you're doing, they're okay".

She says the explosion of content online has "definitely helped" with broadening attitudes to women taking up DIY or a trade.

Anna Moynihan set up TaskHer, a platform connecting female tradies with customers who need jobs done, after feeling frustrated when tradesmen she had booked for renovation work would address her husband rather than her.

Five years ago she says she couldn't find any stock photographs of tradeswomen to use for marketing. Even the word "tradeswoman" would get autocorrected to "tradesman".

"It's those little things that, you know, ultimately you don't feel welcome into that environment.

"It's already hard enough to become a tradeswoman, a woman in an industry where you're massively under-represented."

Enquiries on the site have more than doubled so far this year compared to 2025, while the number of tradeswomen signing up has almost quadrupled, Anna says.

People might prefer a tradeswoman for a range of reasons - industry surveys suggest they may feel more at ease with a woman entering their home , feel a woman would be more respectful, or want to support women working in traditionally male roles.

Anecdotally, Anna says more women are joining her platform after leaving white-collar jobs, adding three Oxford University-educated tradeswomen have signed up in the last month.

She says some had always wanted to take up a trade but felt unable to up until now because of their gender.

Others, she says, want the flexibility of working for themselves in a role less likely to be directly impacted by the rapid advance of AI.

Despite the buzz, women make up a tiny proportion of the UK's construction workforce - around 4%, according to the Federation of Master Builders.

But there are encouraging signs. One in 10 people who started a construction apprenticeship in 2024-25 was a woman, up from around one in 14 five years earlier.

DIY influencer Jasmine hopes women who see online content such as hers will be inspired to give a project a go, or consider entering a trade.

"The more women who are seen online doing these sorts of things, the more normal it becomes."

Anna agrees. "You can't be what you can't see, and anything that shows women and girls that they can do something is fantastic."

articles.title: The start-ups hoping to return battery making to the US
articles.summary: Batteries based on sodium-ion technology could be made in the US with locally sourced materials.
articles.body:
As heatwaves scorched Europe this summer, workers at a US battery company noticed an uptick in demand.

San Diego-based Unigrid sells a nine kilowatt hour battery for people's homes. Sweltering European homeowners were apparently looking for ways of storing power when it was available from the grid at lower rates. They could then run air conditioners more cheaply, off the battery, during the worst heat of the day.

"We have requests coming from Spain, France, Germany, The Netherlands," says Darren Tan, co-founder and chief executive. "We've shipped the first 100 units and [expect to ship] 1,000 before the end of the year."

Unigrid's battery is an emerging technology – it's a sodium ion, rather than lithium ion device. Sodium ion batteries have got energy storage experts excited because they could end up much cheaper to build and operate than lithium ion.

They're potentially less likely to catch fire and should also work in a wider range of temperatures, even down to lows of minus 40C .

But there's a debate over what constitutes the best, and safest, sodium ion battery design. Plus, more than one US company working in this space has floundered in recent years .

China leads the world in sodium ion battery manufacturing at present so US competitors are going to have to work hard to keep up.

The prize that awaits is the possibility of batteries made in the US with 100% US-sourced materials. This is unlike lithium ion batteries, where China dominates the materials supply chain as well as manufacturing.

For Tan, China has helped his company get to market. The Unigrid battery currently uses sodium ion cells made there, rather than in the US. "We can switch back and forth and choose what battery we want to work with," says Tan, explaining that, in future, his firm might source cells from the US – though these may come at a different cost.

There's another consideration. Unigrid's battery contains chromium-3 in its cathode. In a battery, electrons flow from cathode to anode when charging and in the opposite direction when discharging or providing power.

Prof Dame Clare Grey at the University of Cambridge, who is co-founder of battery firm Nyobolt, points out that under certain conditions chromium-3 may form chromium-6, a toxic, cancer-causing material.

"If you're going to go for sodium […] and you're going to sell safety, then don't start putting elements in that are going to raise red flags," she tells the BBC.

Ivana Hasa at the University of Warwick, who has no connection to Unigrid, agrees that it is possible for chromium-3 to form chromium-6 at very high states of charge, though she says this can be mitigated by how voltage is controlled within the battery. "Safety tests reported on the cell chemistry are very promising," she says of Unigrid's tech.

Tan says concerns around toxicity of the battery's materials are "overblown" and emphasises that Unigrid's battery has passed certification and safety tests for sale in Europe and is currently undergoing such evaluations for the US market.

Third-party tests have not been able to get the battery to form chromium-6, he says. "We've tried very hard to try and produce it, we've overcharged it as much as we can... We were unsuccessful in generating chromium-6."

The choice of cathode material, or how the electrolyte – which separates cathode and anode – is formulated are key details influencing the performance and longevity of sodium ion batteries. Some manufacturers are not using chromium for their cathode but hard carbon instead, or sodium iron phosphate pyrophosphate (NFPP).

In general, confidence around sodium ion batteries' reliability has increased during the last few years, says Prof Dame Grey, meaning they are now finding their way into grid storage applications.

Last December, LFP batteries – a relatively cheap form of lithium ion battery – were trading at $81 per kilowatt hour (kWh) whereas Unigrid's sodium ion battery pricing is roughly $100 kWh .

Some companies that spoke to the BBC suggested sodium ion might reach as low as $30 per kWh but analysts say significantly lower costs could be many years away .

Sodium ion batteries are also not as energy dense as lithium ion batteries, meaning they must be slightly bigger and heavier in order to provide the same amount of power.

The technology has been improving on this front in recent years but, even so, you're not likely to see sodium ion cells in small, energy hungry devices such as smartphones. Larger energy storage solutions are where most people expect sodium ion to dominate.

"We think sodium ion […] is going to make up 80% of the market," says David Bell, co-founder and chief executive of Seattle-based Emerald Battery Labs.

Bell declined to share details of the battery design his firm is working on, though he says Emerald too is currently relying on China-sourced sodium ion cells as they develop their initial product: 12 volt auxiliary batteries for vehicles, currently supplied to unnamed commercial fleets in the US.

"We took a look at the market and said 'Hey, no-one's trying to attack this space, let's have Emerald Battery Labs attack it'," says Bell. The firm's next goal is to develop new anodes for US-produced sodium ion cells.

Another company, Peak Energy, based in California and Colorado, announced a partnership with General Motors (GM) in June. The pair aim to develop a US supply chain for sodium ion batteries, in order to enable large-scale energy storage for electricity grids.

Peak Energy is also, at present, relying on China-sourced cells for its first installations, but hopes to help GM launch a US-based production facility in Michigan "by the end of 2028", says Cameron Wiles, president and co-founder. "China does not have an insurmountable lead in sodium ion batteries," he says.

One reason US companies feel they can compete is because of the electricity demand boom from data centres, which are contributing to rising greenhouse gas emissions in the US. Data centre-driven demand is also rising in other places around the world, including the UK .

This is an "opportunity" says Drew Buckley, chief executive at ESS Tech, headquartered in Oregon. He points out that sodium ion batteries could help distribute renewable energy to data centres. And those batteries should be cheaper to run than lithium ion alternatives, since they are not expected to require as much cooling.

ESS Tech is working with Alsym, another US firm that is planning to ship "hundreds" of megawatt hours' worth of sodium ion batteries – made in the US – by 2027.

Hasa says that it will be "challenging" for companies to establish mass production of sodium ion batteries. And she also notes that, while this type of battery is often touted as much safer than lithium ion, they do not come with zero fire risk.

But if any firms can succeed in this space, they could enable new strategic choices, she adds – helping to avoid wastage of renewable electricity and potentially keeping energy costs low. "I'm a strong believer in the technology," says Hasa.

articles.title: Iraq begins high-stakes security balancing act as US troops withdraw
articles.summary: Iraq marks national ‘Sovereignty Days’ as US troops depart, but must navigate risks of new security landscape.
articles.body:
Iraq is set to hold four “Sovereignty Days”, a national holiday marking the complete withdrawal of US troops from the country and underscoring the deep symbolism of the exit after more than two decades of foreign intervention.

Wednesday’s withdrawal deadline affirmed the exodus of a few hundred remaining US soldiers in the country, who have served in advisory roles in a coalition operation against ISIL (ISIS) first launched in 2015.

While the exit plan predates Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, it fits into his wider vision of reasserting Iraqi state authority. That encompasses accelerating efforts to disarm all militias in the country by June 2027, including several powerful pro-Iran groups who have launched attacks throughout the region amid the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) last week, al-Zaidi said his government was “striving to ensure that the state is the ultimate decision-maker in matters of peace and war, and that weapons and tools of power remain in the hands of its constitutional institutions”.

He added, “With the end of the international coalition’s mission in Iraq, we are moving our relationship with our strategic partners to a new phase, moving from military cooperation to economic and development cooperation in service of our common interests.”

Indeed, the US withdrawal appears to be part of a strategy by al-Zaidi to “politically weaken” influential militias , including those linked to Iran, according to Douglas Silliman, the former US ambassador to Iraq and Kuwait.

Those militias have long pointed to the presence of the US military, and other foreign actors like Turkiye, as a pillar justification for maintaining their own weapons stores and chains of command. Some have already indicated they will refuse to hand over their arms.

“The prime minister is clearly trying to build a political case to Iraqis that these forces that are more beholden to Iran, and have used weapons without government authorisation, no longer have a political reason to have those weapons,” said Silliman, who serves as president of the Arab Gulf States Institute.

It is a high-stakes gambit, leaving room for Iran to assert greater influence in the country and opening the door to a potentially catastrophic domestic standoff down the line.

It also creates the potential for increased pressure from the US if Iraq-based groups continue to target Washington’s assets.

“It’s going to be a very difficult series of decisions,” Silliman said. “Both for the militias and for Prime Minister al-Zaidi and his defence team.”

How the Iraqi government navigates the end of the US-led coalition’s deployment, dubbed “Operation Inherent Resolve”, will have wide-ranging implications for the future security of Iraq.

The country has remained relatively stable in recent years following the 2017 territorial defeat of ISIL, despite being enveloped by conflict and insecurity on its borders. That stability has generally persisted since the US began its troop withdrawal in 2020 under US President Donald Trump, with the remaining military personnel consolidating at an airbase in Erbil, in northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region, at the end of 2025.

To be sure, al-Zaidi has already sought to build in some safeguards amid the wider effort to disarm and integrate militias into Iraqi government forces, pushing back on an initial September 30, 2026 deadline to June 2027 to bring all weapons under state control.

Al-Zaidi told The New York Times earlier this month that both the US and Iran-aligned militias have given assurances that they will refrain from any attacks for 90 days following the US withdrawal, in an effort to prevent the situation from devolving in the short term.

Still, Renad Mansour, director of the Iraq Initiative at Chatham House, said militias aligned with Iran’s “axis of resistance” in the region ultimately remain “in full-on war mode, working with the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] in the region. And so they will continue to target US and US interests.”

While al-Zaidi has promised continued integration and cooperation with the US and other Western allies, there is likely disquiet behind the rhetoric, Mansour assessed, with some seeing the US’s erstwhile presence in the country as having served as a bulwark against a wider policy pivot.

“The anxiety from the Iraqi government now is that the US might not need Iraq any more, or might, in the worst case, view Iraq as a pariah state, too close to Iran, and therefore another target,” he said.

The targeting could eventually come in the form of sanctions or in an escalation of US and Israeli strikes on Iraqi territory, Mansour said.

Mohammad Salih, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and an expert on Iraq, also agreed that enthusiasm for the US troop withdrawal was likely more subdued within some segments of the Iraqi government than public statements – and national holidays – suggest.

Salih assessed an underlying wariness to change the security status quo at a time of regional upheaval, pointing to the continued threat from ISIL sleeper cells, shifting cross-border dynamics in a post-Assad Syria, as well as the US-Israel war with Iran.

“The official rhetoric tries to signal that Iraq is more or less fine, that it can take care of itself, and that it seeks stronger commercial and diplomatic ties with the US – that there is no need for the US military presence,” he said.

“But in reality, there is a great deal of concern that Iraq could be the next theatre of some major regional development,” he told Al Jazeera.

The operational implications of the end to the US-led anti-ISIL mission remain difficult to assess.

In the wake of the withdrawal, the two countries appear to be reverting to a 2008 Strategic Framework and Security Agreement, signed under the administration of US President George W Bush, Salih said. The deal pledges continued, if non-binding, US security support for Iraq.

Neither the Iraqi government nor the Pentagon have given a clear picture of what shape security cooperation could take going forward, particularly when it comes to the intelligence and logistical support that buoyed ISIL’s territorial defeat.

However, a regional source with knowledge of the situation told Al Jazeera the relationship is “likely to become less centred on a visible military footprint and more focused on intelligence, training, technical support, capacity-building and institutional cooperation”.

The source called the change a “test of whether a relationship built for a period of military intervention can evolve into a more conventional partnership between sovereign states”.

Several experts noted that Iraqi security forces – including its military, police, counterterrorism forces, and militias who fought as part of the Popular Mobilisation Forces – have taken major strides in responding to ISIL. That may potentially minimise any operational fallout from the physical exit of US personnel.

“There are real capabilities and real experience in the Iraqi security forces. People I talk to in the military are quite confident that they can take on most threats against the sovereignty of Iraq,” former Ambassador Silliman said.

But while the Iraqi parliament approved a partial cabinet in May, several key security roles, including minister of defence, remain unfilled.

The Iraqi government also continues to lack a substantial air defence capability of its own, which could prove a major weakness if the domestic security situation were to spiral, Silliman said.

“This is one area where there will be vulnerabilities because it is clear that the pro-Iran militias have been willing to use drones and rockets and missiles against Iraqi targets inside Iraq, and as of right now, the Iraqi military doesn’t really have a way to defend against that,” he said.

Kurdish officials have been among the most vocal critics of the US withdrawal, pointing to a barrage of attacks on Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region by Iran and Iran-aligned militias thwarted by US anti-missile and anti-drone weapons this year.

While experts say the US may maintain limited air-defence capabilities in Iraq to protect its diplomatic assets, the military has reportedly removed its Erbil-based Patriot and C-RAM defensive systems from the country as part of the withdrawal.

“The threat is real – we are vulnerable, we are being attacked,” Masrour Barzani, the prime minister of the Kurdistan Regional Government, told the Financial Times this week.

“Now, to be left alone without any, let’s say, appropriate defensive system,” he added, “it’s shameful.”

To be sure, the withdrawal of the remaining US troops is only one step in a larger, years-long effort to transform the US-Iraqi relationship from military to economic. Following the 2003 invasion as part of the US-led “global war on terror”, the US had initially withdrawn troops in 2011, only to redeploy them amid the rise of ISIL.

Speaking at the UNGA, al-Zaidi promised an economic “renaissance”, pledging to boost Iraq’s petrochemical industry and build new fossil fuel delivery routes beyond the Strait of Hormuz. The constriction of traffic in the strait amid the US-Israel war with Iran has had an outsized impact on Iraq, with its oil output dropping by as much as 60 percent in March.

For his part, during a meeting at the White House in July, US PresidentTrump pledged “a lot of deals” to come with Iraq, pointing to the country’s vast oil reserves.

Hamzeh Hadad, an adjunct fellow with the Middle East Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security, said there were no immediate signs the US planned a wholesale shift in its approach towards Iraq, which still houses the largest US embassy in the world in Baghdad and the largest consulate in Erbil.

But deeper economic integration may be stalled in the short term.

“It is important to note, for this to happen successfully, the situation in the region needs to improve,” Hadad said.

“Conflict around Iraq will always make economic cooperation more difficult. Not to mention, conflict gives armed groups an excuse to continue to exist.”

Lahib Higel, the deputy director of the MENA programme at the International Crisis Group, called on Washington to focus on cooperation, while avoiding “pressuring al-Zaidi into a military confrontation against pro-Iran groups that he is unlikely to win”.

“A better approach would be for the US to preserve bilateral security cooperation and support his efforts to strengthen state institutions over time,” Higel said in a social media post.

“Washington cannot dictate Baghdad’s relationship with Tehran, nor can Tehran dictate Iraq’s relationship with Washington,” she said. “What Iraq instead needs is the space to find its own balance.”

articles.title: Venezuelan man shot by ICE officer in Texas is charged with assault
articles.summary: Wilber Rafael Garces Perez has disputed the government’s account of what led to his shooting during a DoorDash delivery.
articles.body:
A Venezuelan asylum seeker who was shot in the back by a United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Texas is facing a federal assault charge, after prosecutors accused him of striking the officer with his car’s side-view mirror.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, appeared in federal court in Austin on Tuesday, where he was charged with assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer. He could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

The charge stems from a September 20 encounter that began while Garces Perez was making a DoorDash food delivery near a shopping centre in Austin, the Texas state capital.

A federal complaint filed on Monday says immigration officers noticed that Garces Perez’s car had its emergency lights flashing, and they ran a database check. They found it was registered to Garces Perez, who was subject to a final order of removal from the US.

When the officers approached, Garces Perez handed over his driver’s license through a partially opened window but did not get out of the car, the complaint says. He asked the officers to wait until his wife could arrive to retrieve the vehicle.

Court documents describe the exchange up to that point as “pleasant and not aggressive”.

About a minute later, however, court documents say Garces Perez “abruptly” closed his window and drove off, striking one of the officers in the torso with his driver’s side mirror.

That officer chased Garces Perez in his own vehicle and caught up with him a short time later. In the complaint, the officer alleges that Garces Perez then tried to drive into him, prompting him to open fire.

There is no publicly available footage showing the events described in the complaint, including the shooting.

Videos, however, have circulated online showing the shooting’s aftermath, with Garces Perez injured in his car.

The complaint relies on unreleased body-camera footage from one of the two ICE officers who stopped Garces Perez.

The second officer was not wearing a body camera, according to the affidavit. That officer says he was struck by Garces Perez’s side mirror and later shot him.

Garces Perez, however, gave federal investigators a different account of the moments immediately before he was shot.

He told investigators that, after a brief chase, a law enforcement SUV struck his car, causing it to spin around, according to the affidavit. He said the officer then opened fire, shooting him in the back.

Garces Perez has been held in a detention facility in south Texas since the shooting.

His lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said on Sunday the bullet was still lodged in his body and that he has a fractured clavicle. In a social media post, Lincoln-Goldfinch explained that his supporters were worried he could develop sepsis or suffer permanent damage if he didn’t undergo surgery soon.

The Department of Homeland Security has argued, however, that Garces Perez is receiving adequate medical care.

Garces Perez’s legal team is also seeking to stop his removal from the US.

The Venezuelan national entered the US in 2024 through CBP One, an online programme expanded under former President Joe Biden to allow asylum seekers to make appointments with immigration authorities at the US-Mexico border.

Trump ended the programme on his first day back in office, accusing the app of contributing to an immigration crisis in the US. His administration has since relaunched CBP One as CBP Home, a self-deportation portal.

Lincoln-Goldfinch has said Garces Perez was legally seeking asylum in the US and had a valid work permit. She has asserted that he was ordered to be deported after missing an immigration court hearing because the notice had been sent to an old address.

Garces Perez is due back before a federal immigration judge on Wednesday for a separate hearing on whether he can remain in the country.

The case comes amid a surge in immigration enforcement during Trump’s second term, with ICE reporting more than 50,000 arrests in both July and August.

articles.title: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
articles.summary: Ukraine's remaining steelworks, a vital part of its economy, have all but ground to a halt because of relentless attacks.
articles.body:
Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city.

"Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says.

Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September.

"All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains.

Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded.

"We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC.

At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again.

Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times.

This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia.

Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another.

Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko.

Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action.

"Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far."

The damage to the metals industry could have devastating consequences for Ukraine's economy and society.

Ukraine had 12 metallurgical plants before losing parts of its industrial heartland in the east shortly after the start of hostilities with Russia in 2014.

By 2018, there were just nine, and three years into the full-scale war in 2025 that number had fallen to six. Among those lost were the Azovstal and Illich plants in Mariupol, Ukraine's south-eastern city captured after a months-long Russian siege.

Among the steel-making cities caught up in Russia's recent missile campaign is President Volodymyr Zelensky's home city of Kryvyi Rih.

On 25 September, Ukraine's biggest steelworks, Arcelor Mittal Kryvyi Rih, announced it was unable to reopen after repeated attacks over five weeks, praising the bravery of its workers, five of whom had died.

Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished?

Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs.

The situation, he admitted, was very difficult.

"It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things."

Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center.

"In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC.

"This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (£1.5bn-£2.3bn) a year on average."

If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming."

The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction.

Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia.

Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware.

"We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv.

There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added.

Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon.

Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery.

"Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't."

EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine.

But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat.

His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed.

"This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

articles.title: ‘Nothing is justifying this’: Qatar’s PM slams Israel’s atrocities in Gaza
articles.summary: Qatar’s top diplomat says Israel has undermined Doha’s efforts to broker a ceasefire in Gaza from ‘day one’.
articles.body:
Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani has condemned Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, saying whoever is responsible for the devastation in the besieged Palestinian territory is a “war criminal”.

Sheikh Mohammed, who is also Qatar’s foreign minister, made the remark on Tuesday on “Piers Morgan Uncensored” when asked about the nature of Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip.

He described the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, as “a massacre” that “should be condemned”. He called for accountability for the perpetrators of that attack, but said the Israeli response was unjustified.

“Hospitals have been targeted, schools have been targeted. Whatever the justifications and the arguments, nothing is justifying this,” he added.

Sheikh Mohammed also criticised Israel’s near-daily violations of the “ceasefire” that took effect in October 2025, saying more than 1,400 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip had been killed since.

“There is more occupied territory – almost 70 percent of the Strip has been occupied and not allowed by the Israeli forces. They are not fulfilling their commitments of this agreement,” he said. “This is just showing that they have different intentions.”

He said Qatar’s efforts to broker a ceasefire had been repeatedly “undermined” by Israel “from day one of the war”.

He also condemned Israel’s strike on the Qatari capital, Doha, in 2025, which targeted senior Hamas officials who had gathered for negotiations. The attack, which caused a deadly explosion, was an unprecedented violation of Qatar’s sovereignty.

“We were attacked by Israel while we were mediating and trying to push for Trump’s proposal at that time in Doha,” he said, referring to US President Donald Trump. “It was unacceptable and condemned. It’s setting a precedent of attacking the mediator that has never happened throughout the wars in history.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin “Netanyahu has crossed the line”, he added, “like he has crossed other lines before that”.

Sheikh Mohammed said that serving as a mediator had not been easy, but that he believed quiet diplomacy was the most effective way to make progress.

Qatar has also been playing a mediatory role, along with Pakistan, between the United States and Iran following the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran.

“We are trying to do our best to give the best advice to the US government on how to reach a solution, as well as to the Iranians,” he said.

Sheikh Mohammed said that three matters needed to be resolved to end the war.

These are: an agreement on Tehran’s right to “peaceful nuclear power” and the removal of sanctions; agreement on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz according to international law; and reform of regional security arrangements, including the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and Iran.

The last, he said, “wouldn’t happen without dialogue between Iran and GCC and setting the principles of what a good neighbourhood relationship should be”.

That should include, he said, “non-interference in each other’s affairs” and “non-aggression” against each other.

He added that if the region were to “build an area of common interest where we work together in areas of energy and economy, and trade and business”, it would “allow the chance for this region to unleash its potential”.

articles.title: Spain proposes ban on evictions as ousted 87-year-old accepts offer to return home
articles.summary: Hundreds of people remained camped in one of Madrid’s main squares Tuesday to protest Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher last Wednesday.
articles.body: MADRID — Spain’s coalition government said it had agreed to proposals including banning evictions until 2030 to address the country’s housing crisis, as the 87-year-old woman whose forced removal last week triggered protests accepted an offer to return home. Hundreds of people remained camped in one of Madrid’s main squares on Tuesday to protest Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher last Wednesday. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes. Health Minister Mónica García said the ruling Socialists reached an agreement with junior partner Sumar on Tuesday for a set of new measures, including rolling over contracts until 2028 and banning so-called vulture funds from the housing market. However, the minority government faces an uphill battle to secure support in a fragmented parliament. The government was seeking to broaden the definition of what constitutes a vulture fund beyond large private equity funds to any fund or company that buys housing for speculation, Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez said at a news conference, naming Urbagestión, the small company that evicted Abascal, as an example of a firm that might fall into that category. Urbagestión didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The measures will be divided into two decrees to be voted on in parliament on Friday, with the majority in a first decree. The “final sticking point” of automatic contract rollover is in a second decree, Social Affairs Minister Pablo Bustinduy said at a news conference. ‘Time to intervene’ “It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds,” García wrote on X. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing on all measures and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain. “We all agreed that evictions — where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros — obviously need to be stopped,” Junts parliamentary spokesperson Míriam Nogueras said on RTVE. “Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property — putting them all in the same basket — is a mistake,” she added. Madrid’s tenants’ union criticized the government’s decision to split the measures into two decrees and said the Madrid encampment and others across Spain would continue until their full demands were met, with further demonstrations planned. The lawyer for pensioner Abascal said on Tuesday that Urbagestión, the fund that owns her apartment, had offered a preliminary agreement that will allow her return to her home, paying 30% of her pension over the next eight years, equivalent to around €500 a month. This would see her paying a similar level as prior to the eviction. “She should never have been forced to leave,” Beatriz Duro told reporters. “I hope this case serves to provide a collective response to the housing crisis.”
