articles.title: Asian benchmarks mostly rise despite ongoing worries about Iran war
articles.summary: Mediators continued to work with the U.S. and Iran on reaching a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz. President Donald Trump over the weekend rejected an offer from Tehran to reopen the key waterway.
articles.body: TOKYO — Asian shares rose in early Wednesday trading, boosted by optimism about artificial intelligence and computer chips despite ongoing worries about the war in Iran. Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 jumped 1.3% in morning trading to 66,318.81. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.9% to 8,791.30. South Korea’s Kospi lost earlier gains to be little changed, up less than 0.1% at 6,875.84. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.1% to 24,551.47, while the Shanghai Composite rose 0.3% to 3,843.26. SoftBank Group Corp., which invests in OpenAI, surged about 6% in Tokyo morning trading. Also gaining were Japanese chip-related stocks like Renesas Electronics and Rohm Co. Stocks closed modestly lower on Wall Street on Tuesday as another increase in long-term Treasury yields weighed on the market. The S&P 500 slipped 0.2% after wavering between modest gains and losses for much of the day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.3%, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.1%. Major indexes shifted lower after a quiet morning as rising bond yields undercut much of the heavy lifting being done by several technology behemoths. Nvidia, the market’s most influential stock, gave up an early gain and closed 0.7% lower. Broadcom rose 1.6%. Oil prices are swinging sharply as the U.S. war with Iran drags on, helping push Treasury yields to their highest levels in 24 years. Benchmark U.S. crude added 0.23% to $89.59 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, edged up 0.87% to $103.48 a barrel. Brent is well above the roughly $72 it cost before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Mediators continued to work with the United States and Iran on reaching a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz. President Donald Trump over the weekend rejected an offer from Tehran to reopen the key waterway. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 5.25% from 5.24% late Monday. It reached 5.28% earlier Tuesday, touching its highest level since 2002, according to Tradeweb. All told, the S&P 500 fell 12.85 points to 7,670.84. The Dow dropped 131.59 points to 51,349.92, and the Nasdaq gave up 22.84 points to close at 26,797.54. Wall Street will see several big economic updates this week that could help investors and the Federal Reserve get a better sense of where inflation is headed. U.S. inflation rates have remained stubbornly above 3% most of the year, well above the Fed’s target rate of 2%. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise its benchmark interest rate again at its next meeting in October. “While it is easy to focus on the macroeconomic headwinds of bond yields and oil, the underlying U.S. economy remains remarkably resilient,” said Tina Teng, market analyst at MooMoo, a global financial technology and online brokerage company. In currency trading, the U.S. dollar declined to 156.75 Japanese yen from 157.27 yen. The euro cost $1.1335, down from $1.1347.

articles.title: Utah man released after decades on death row as DNA evidence excludes him from 1985 killing
articles.summary: A Utah man who spent decades on death row was released on bail after DNA evidence excluded him from the 1985 killing of a police chief's aunt.
articles.body: A Utah man who has spent decades on death row after he was convicted of killing a police chief's aunt has been released after prosecutors said newly analyzed DNA evidence excluded him as the source of DNA recovered from key pieces of evidence in the case. Douglas Stewart Carter, 71, was let out on bail late Monday over objections from the victim's family. He must wear a GPS monitor while he awaits a new trial in the killing of Eva Olesen, who was found tied up, stabbed and shot inside her Provo home on Feb. 27, 1985, during what investigators suspected was a robbery. A judge ordered him not to have any contact with Olesen's family. The Utah Supreme Court ordered a new trial last year, pointing to misconduct by investigators. MAN ‘FRAMED’ IN ‘SATANIC’ MURDER FREED AFTER 22 YEARS WINS $24M AS REAL KILLER STILL UNKNOWN Carter has maintained his innocence and argues that he was coerced into a signed confession. No physical evidence linked Carter to the crime scene, but the jury convicted him based on the confession and the testimony of two witnesses who claimed he bragged about killing Olesen, although those witnesses later recanted. A DNA analysis received on Sept. 22 excluded Carter as a possible match to blood found on a doorknob and genetic material recovered from the handle of a knife used to stab Olesen. Judge Derek Pullan said those findings further undermined the case against Carter, but noted that a jury could still say that he killed Olesen. "This is going to be a lot for him," Carter's son, Tyler Anger, said on Monday as he waited for his father after his release was ordered. Carter will be placed in an extended stay hotel located near Anger, who was adopted by another family as an infant and did not learn about his father's conviction until years later, according to Carter's attorney, Neal Hamilton. Carter will need therapy to deal with his extended incarceration, Hamilton said. "If the state of Utah had their way, he would have been executed 15, 20 years ago before we discovered the misconduct," Hamilton said. Hamilton also urged prosecutors to seek dismissal of an aggravated murder charge still pending against Carter. NEW HAMPSHIRE SUPREME COURT OVERTURNS ADAM MONTGOMERY'S MURDER CONVICTION IN DAUGHTER HARMONY'S DEATH A two-month retrial was planned next year, but county prosecutors withdrew a notice last week that they wanted to pursue the death penalty. Utah County prosecutor Erwin Petilos told the judge on Monday that reassessing Carter's bail was "necessary and fair" as the state continues to examine the remaining evidence in the case. Carter was living with his mother in Utah when Olesen was killed. By April of 1985, Carter had fled Utah, believing he was a suspect in an unrelated assault case, court documents show. He was detained two months later in Nashville, where he signed a confession while under interrogation by a Provo detective. Carter said later that his confession was coerced, saying he falsely admitted to the crime after police repeatedly threatened him. He was convicted and sentenced to death after a trial in which the defense called no witnesses to testify. Carter was sentenced to death again after a 1992 retrial, and courts in Utah later denied multiple appeals from Carter's legal team. In 2011, the two witnesses from Carter's original trial were tracked down in Mexico, admitting they had been told to lie in court and had received cash and gifts from police in exchange for their testimonies. They said police told them not to disclose the payments and that police and prosecutors threatened them and their son with deportation if they did not implicate Carter in the killing. More than a decade of legal fights ensued before the Utah Supreme Court stepped in last year and ordered a new trial, citing "multiple instances of intentional misconduct" by police and a prosecutor. A DNA analysis of the evidence was conducted in response to that order, and prosecutors said the results arrived last week, which excluded Carter from the crime. Prosecutors declined to say whether they will use the DNA evidence to search for other suspects with matching DNA. Attorneys for Carter, who is Black, have said witnesses saw a White man fleeing the crime scene and that an investigator suppressed evidence that could implicate other suspects, including the victim’s husband, Orla Olesen. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Prosecutors were close to filing charges against the husband, but a Provo police lieutenant urged them not to so he could continue investigating, according to the defense attorneys. Carter was then identified as a suspect, according to court documents. Orla Olesen, who died in 2009, told police he found his wife dead in their home, partially undressed and with her hands tied behind her back. Theresa Olesen, a daughter-in-law of Eva Olesen, said during the bond hearing on Monday that her family had "serious concerns" about Carter's release. "By golly we were hoping for a concrete match," Olesen said of the DNA analysis. "It doesn't mean he wasn't there." "We just want justice for Eva. And if he had any part of it we want that to be known," she added. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Choosing financial stability over dreams is 'heart-breaking'
articles.summary: Young people struggling to make ends meet respond to the government's Your First Home scheme.
articles.body:
The prime minister used the plight of young people unable to rely on the "bank of mum and dad" as a curtain-raiser for Labour's annual conference.

The Your First Home scheme will offer a government-backed loan of 20% of the purchase price - with a minimum deposit of 2.5%.

But how tough are things at the moment for young people who have left school and want to make their way in the world?

Chari, 19, from Hertfordshire, spent some of her childhood in care but has just started at university and has ambitions to qualify as a doctor of psychology.

The challenge at the moment is just getting through the next few years, she says.

"I receive universal credit and that's usually what I would use to pay for my housing in Hertfordshire, but they've cut it off this month because I'm moving to university and they think SFE [the student loan] will cover it.

"SFE is delayed, so I have no money this month whatsoever - I'm three days in and already I'm in debt."

She added: "I'm dipping into savings I had planned to afford a future for myself just to get by now.

"As a care leaver, you don't really get that chance to save money for your future or make future plans."

Chari believes her dream of a doctorate may have to be put on hold while she pursues a career - and a salary - in banking.

"It's heart-breaking," she said, adding: "I don't think somebody should have to choose financial stability over pursuing their dream."

Elliot, 18, is also from Hertfordshire and is living with their parents, but wants to move on.

"I've been looking for places because I'm in college and I plan on going to uni, but it's just that things keep rising and the bills keep getting more and more," they said.

"I don't think I've ever expected to be able to buy a house at all. It would be nice to own my own place, but will I actually earn enough to be able to?"

As they turn 19 within a couple of months, Elliot believes they will have to pay for their studies.

"It's about £1,500 to £2,000 just for the course and I've got to get there and back every day," they said.

"In the area that I live, one of the main things is if you don't have the education, you're probably not going to get out of the place.

"It's quite a low-income area. I would like to go to uni but I think 'can I afford it?'"

The government said the Your First Home scheme would "help tackle the deposit barrier for first-time buyers who would be unable to afford their first home otherwise, building on the government's existing work to help more young people and families onto the housing ladder".

The Conservatives warned that the policy could leave first-time buyers taking on more debt and risked "pushing up the price of new homes".

But the prime minister said it would aim to help those who did not have support from the "bank of mum and dad".

Burnham said: "Too many young people are struggling with the cost of housing, with many giving up hope of ever having a home to call their own.

"So we will step in to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder."

articles.title: Anglian Water hopes to consult on desalination by 2027
articles.summary: The company says two proposed desalination plants will help it secure future water supplies.
articles.body:
Anglian Water has revealed more information about proposals for two desalination plants in a bid to secure water supplies for the region.

In January, the company awarded a £29m contract to partnership TYPSA-Stantec - desalination and engineering firms - to develop plans for the plants in Norfolk and Lincolnshire.

Anglian Water said that, without intervention, it estimated a daily shortfall of approximately half of the current volume of water entering the network by 2050, in what is the "driest and fastest growing" region of the UK.

"The benefits of seawater desalination are that it provides a climate-resilient source of water," said Anglian Water.

"Whilst traditional water resources are dependent on rainfall and river flows, desalinated water comes from the sea, meaning it is available all year to support supplies during periods of drought and increasing water scarcity."

The water company said the desalination plans, together with the creation of two new reservoirs , were part of a 2025-2030 £11bn investment plan.

Anglian Water hoped to have "a shortlist of potential sites for both desalination plants by the end of this year before preferred sites are identified in 2027".

Further consultation and engagement would then take place as "the plans evolve", the company said.

Caister-on-Sea in Norfolk and Mablethorpe in Lincolnshire have previously been mentioned as potential sites .

Seawater desalination is a relatively new technology within the UK water industry, and the two proposed new plants would be the first of their kind in the Anglian Water region.

The plants will work by abstracting water from the North Sea, using pre-treatment, reverse osmosis and remineralisation, before blending treated water into the supply.

The company said brine waste would be dispersed via a long sea outfall and well-designed diffusing systems.

The release of brine back into the sea is controversial, with some concerned about the potential impact on the marine environment.

The highly salty water left after desalination is toxic to marine life and today's desalination facilities produce huge quantities of it .

The area Anglian Water serves spans from as far north as Grimsby in Lincolnshire to Southend-on-Sea, Essex and from Northampton and Milton Keynes in the west to Lowestoft and Great Yarmouth in the east.

Anglian Water said the region was growing and it was adding 70,000 new customers every year.

Currently, water supplies remain under pressure following successive heatwaves and prolonged dry weather.

In some areas, particularly Norwich and Norfolk, Anglian Water said it was concerned as rivers it used to extract drinking water were running exceptionally low, such as the River Wensum.

In the East of England, half of the water supply comes from groundwater aquifers .

articles.title: Redmere Wind farm near RAF bases could invite sabotage - MP
articles.summary: Nick Timothy, MP for West Suffolk, questions the plan's suitability near two US Air Force bases.
articles.body:
Building a major wind farm near two air bases could invite "sabotage" from hostile nations, an MP has warned.

Nick Timothy, the Conservative MP for West Suffolk, questioned the suitability of building Redmere Wind Farm near the key US Air Force (USAF) bases of RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall, which are in his constituency.

Up to 32 turbines could be built at the site which encompasses the Suffolk, Norfolk and Cambridgeshire borders.

Vattenfall, the Swedish state-owned developer behind the plans, which are at an early stage, said it would be consulting residents about its proposal.

The firm said the turbines - which might be up to 721ft (220m) tall - could power nearly 220,000 homes a year when operational.

The final plans are due to be submitted in autumn 2027.

"I have warned repeatedly that battery energy storage systems near important airbases is an invitation for hostile states and others to commit acts of sabotage," Timothy said.

"There are also questions about building an enormous wind farm near the bases."

His concerns were echoed by Tristan Gale, Reform UK's cabinet member for planning at Suffolk County Council, who said: "These things are in the flight path and they are huge, they are massive.

"They are going to affect the radars for an air station."

Guidance published on the Ministry of Defence website states it should be consulted if a proposed turbine is 11m (36ft) high or more.

"Wind turbines can adversely affect a number of MoD operations including radars, seismological recording equipment, communications facilities, naval operations and low flying," it said.

Due to the scale of the project, Vattenfall can bypass the local planning authority and instead seek permission directly from central government.

Sites surrounding the Shippea Hill railway station have been earmarked for the development.

A Vattenfall spokesman said: "Redmere wind farm could make a major contribution to cleaner, more secure energy systems while bringing jobs and investment to the local area.

"Vattenfall is working on design proposals and environmental work, so we want local people to meet the team, learn more and help shape the project from the outset."

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has been contacted for comment, as has RAF Lakenheath.

articles.title: Sunderland Pianoforte Society holds last recital at Winter Gardens
articles.summary: A last recital is given on a Steinway piano before moving from Sunderland Museum and Winter Gardens.
articles.body:
A piano society founded during World War Two has held its last recital at the museum it called home.

Sunderland Pianoforte Society has for decades hosted performances at the city's Museum and Winter Gardens, which shut in August ahead of a two-year refurbishment.

Despite the closure, on Tuesday the society was given the chance to hold one last performance on its Model D Steinway, which it has kept at the museum since the 1960s.

With the society moving to Hope Street Xchange in the city centre, Chair Eileen Bown thanked the museum for a "long and really happy relationship" but said it was unclear whether the group and piano would be able to return after the revamped facility reopened.

The piano, made in the Louis XVI fashion in light walnut, was made sometime around 1902 in Hamburg, Germany, and is believed to be one of only six built in that style.

Following years of borrowing instruments, the society obtained the instrument in the late 1960s at the recommendation of pianist Ronald Smith.

"The society started in 1943," said Bown.

"That was just a group of like-minded people who enjoyed playing the piano, then it just grew and it's still here today, which is amazing really.

"This is the end of an era and the beginning of a new era."

The £13.6m upgrade of the museum, including a new entrance and galleries, is currently planned to be finished in time for a reopening in late 2028.

articles.title: Customers in the South taking risks with heating oil orders, firm says
articles.summary: Customers in Berkshire and Hampshire are leaving it late to refill their tanks, an oil firm says.
articles.body:
Heating oil customers who are worried about the cost are taking risks by delaying orders in the hope of a price fall, a firm has warned.

Marsh Fuels, which supplies heating oil in Berkshire and Hampshire, said its sales were lower than expected as colder weather approaches.

However, the firm said customers could run out of oil or expose themselves to even higher bills by waiting.

UK heating oil prices have risen by about 75% since the start of the Iran conflict on 28 February, according to the BoilerJuice website .

Dave Marsh from the Newbury-based firm said: "We're coming into autumn and we would expect to be busier than we are.

"And so we've made the assumption that customers are hanging on, trying to eke out that little bit of oil they've still got left in the bottom of their tank, hoping for the price to dip.

"The problem is that can be quite risky. If we get a cold snap and the customers are lower than they think they are, they may suddenly be urgent."

Andrew Illingworth, who buys oil on behalf of residents in Broughton, Hampshire, said he was handling fewer orders than normal for the time of year.

"A lot of them are holding off at the moment," he said.

"They're hoping that it's going to go back down again, but who knows at the moment."

Chris Wheeler, from Bucklebury, Berkshire, said the price volatility, including surges and dips, was "frustrating".

"You never know what's going to happen," he said. "Except at the moment all you can expect is that the price is going to go up.

"So we're trying to manage our purchases so that we can buy it when it's at its cheapest."

Ellen Fraser, energy expert at the Baringa consultancy, said she would buy oil now.

She told the Money Box programme on BBC Radio 4: "We're expecting those prices to stay high until at least April and May, which is obviously far too late to fill the tank."

The Fuel Distribution Association (UKIFDA) previously said customers should prepare for periods of increased demand, severe weather or unexpected delivery delays.

Chief executive Ken Mackness said: "The events we saw earlier this year demonstrated how quickly international developments can affect wholesale energy markets."

In March, the government announced a £50m emergency fund to help struggling families with heating oil costs.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The five-day Uttar Pradesh International Trade Show (UPITS) 2026 concluded on Tuesday with the signing of 4,400 Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) worth approximately Rs 6,500 crore (around USD 680 million), while potential business worth around Rs 15,500 crore was estimated from business enquiries received during the event.The fourth edition of the trade show was held at the India Expo Centre & Mart from September 25 to 29. Total B2B meetings increased by 31.12 per cent from 31,650 in 2025 to 41,500 this year. Sessions with foreign buyers in the RBSM section rose by 123.1 per cent from 6,050 to 13,500, while meetings in the main exhibition area grew by 9.38 per cent.The number of MoUs signed rose by 12.82 per cent from 3,900 to 4,400, while their estimated value rose by 142.54 per cent from Rs 2,680 crore (USD 425 million) to Rs 6,500 crore (USD 680 million). Business enquiries also recorded a 24 per cent rise, leading to an estimated potential business increase from Rs 12,500 crore to Rs 15,500 crore.International participation expanded from a single partner country, Russia, in the previous edition to six partner nations this year, namely Russia, Austria, Japan, Singapore, Belarus, and Vietnam. Overseas delegations engaged with sectors including manufacturing, information technology, electronics, textiles, and agri-food processing.Chief minister Yogi Adityanath's ambitious "One District, One Dish (ODOC)" scheme remained the main attraction among foreign and domestic buyers throughout the event. articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani is Samajwadi Party's 'surprise' candidate for the Rajya Sabha polls along with party's secretary general Prof Ram Gopal
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani is Samajwadi Party's 'surprise' candidate for the Rajya Sabha polls along with party's secretary general Prof Ram Gopal Yadav. Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani is the Group President of Reliance Industries and considered to be very close to the Ambani family. He is also a sports administrator. articles.title: Endometriosis trial gives hope to millions of women in pain like me
articles.summary: A £2.3m study will look at whether a personalised pain management plan can improve the quality of life of women who have the debilitating condition.
articles.body:
Charlotte McCann has been dealing with severe pain from endometriosis since she was 14. It became so intolerable as an adult she had to leave her chosen career.

She would wake up in the night vomiting, and on some days Charlotte found she could not stand or get out of bed.

It is a myth that endometriosis is a painful period condition - rather, it is a system-wide inflammatory disease where cells, similar to those which line the womb, start to grow in other parts of the body. This can be on the bowel or in the lungs - and the cells multiply, creating raw and angry sores.

Those affected can wait years for diagnosis, and there is no cure - meaning women are left grappling with debilitating pain that can affect their relationships, work, education and mental health.

Now age 27, Charlotte hopes a new pain management programme for the condition, which is being trialled as part of a £2.3m study, might help others in her position.

The UK-wide study, led by the University of Aberdeen and NHS Grampian, will include pain medication alongside other treatments such as physiotherapy, and will investigate whether a personalised plan can improve quality of life.

Women can wait years for an endometriosis diagnosis. New tech could change that

Emma Barnett: We can't ignore this disease that leaves one in 10 women like me in agony

Charlotte, from Huntly in Aberdeenshire, is currently living with stage 4 endometriosis .

She had to abandon her career in corporate finance due to the pain, and now works as a freelance pet-sitter when she can.

"I would wake up in the night vomiting and I was always worried that maybe my appendix had burst or I had a kidney infection or something like that," she recalled.

"The pain would come on so strong, I wouldn't be able to even sit up straight, I wouldn't be able to stand up.

"It was heavily disrupting my life. I couldn't focus on anything, and I couldn't sleep or eat because of the pain.

"There's no way I could continue my nine-to-five job when I could barely sit up."

Charlotte said she had years of not knowing what was wrong, until an MRI scan confirmed endometriosis.

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

It affected her bladder, and has spread to other parts of her body.

"I am now on very strong opioid painkillers to try to get on top of the pain, but they make me feel very sick, to the point I can't eat, so I have lost a lot of weight now as well," she said.

Charlotte described being in so much pain that there are days when she cannot get out of bed.

She also has to use walking aids to get around due to the pain in her back brought on by her endometriosis symptoms.

She tried surgery to remove the tissue in question, but the symptoms returned.

Asked about the new trial, Charlotte said she was optimistic.

"Endometriosis has had a huge impact on my life, and I am delighted to hear that they are looking at new ways to help the millions of women who are suffering with this every single day."

Preparatory work has now begun for the five-year study, which is being funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR).

Once participants are recruited, they will take part in a 12-week personalised programme - called an endometriosis-specific pain management programme (e-PMP).

The project will evaluate whether this strategy can offer more effective treatment for women who find their pain is not adequately controlled by surgery or medication.

It includes cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)-informed psychotherapy, specialist physiotherapy, guidance on relationships, intimacy and communication, and medication to reduce side effects.

Pre-menopausal women will either receive the new programme alongside existing standard care, or existing standard care alone, with the results of each approach then compared.

Eligible participants will be recruited to the study by their specialist.

Consultant gynaecologist Dr Lucky Saraswat, an honorary senior lecturer at the university, and lead for Aberdeen Endometriosis Centre at NHS Grampian, is heading the study.

"Endometriosis is one of the most common yet under researched causes of chronic pain," she said. "Many women continue to suffer even after surgery or medication.

"This study will help us understand whether a tailored, interdisciplinary pain management programme can offer meaningful, long term improvements in quality of life.

"If effective, e-PMP could become a vital new treatment option, particularly for women who wish to avoid repeated surgery or hormonal therapies, or who are planning a pregnancy."

Alongside the clinical results, the study will also aim to assess cost effectiveness.

Prof Anthony Gordon, director of NIHR's health technology assessment programme, said many women could face years of "agonising" symptoms with few long-term options.

"High-quality research is essential to break this cycle and deliver treatment that addresses the full, complex impact of endometriosis," he said.

"By evaluating tailored, non-surgical pain management, this trial could revolutionise care - providing desperately needed support, improving daily lives, and offering long-term relief when standard treatments haven't worked."

Emma Cox, chief executive of Endometriosis UK, added: "Symptoms of endometriosis including chronic pelvic pain can have a significant impact on someone's physical and mental health, and research is vital to helping improve management and treatment options.

"We welcome this much-needed research and look forward to working with the team to see how an endometriosis specific pain management programme could support those with the disease in the future."

articles.title: Drop in donations puts Sheffield community pantry at risk of closure
articles.summary: St Paul's Pantry in Norton Lees say things are looking "pretty grim" without support.
articles.body:
Volunteers at a community pantry say they fear they may have to close unless they can bring in additional donations of money and food.

Tina Sampson-Smith from St Paul's community pantry, in Norton Lees, Sheffield, said a drop off in donations and a rise in demand had left them in a precarious situation.

Asked how the coming weeks and months looked she replied: "They look pretty grim at the moment."

According to the Trussell Trust more than 2.2m food parcels were given out in England in 2025, a 56% rise on 2019.

Sampson-Smith said: "I looked at our freezers yesterday and the majority of them are off because we do not have the food stock in them.

"It's always tough from September to November, but this year is tougher than ever."

She said, in recent weeks, one day the pantry had 204 people turn up in need of support.

"Food poverty is really, really high at the moment and it's a never-ending battle to get food because our supermarkets haven't got the stock to give us," she said.

Co-founder Jay Judge said: "It's a day to day battle

"[There's] more and more people in food poverty, those that you see and those that you don't see.

"For every person that turns up at the pantry there's a family behind that.

"We might be seeing over 200 people coming through the door but it's feeding a lot more people than that."

Sampson-Smith added: "We provided school lunches during the school holidays, but at this point in time we've nothing in our freezers to do that for half term."

Jenny Farrall‑Bird, area manager for charity the Trussel Trust, said this time of year was especially demanding for food banks.

She said some families on the lowest incomes were going to have to make decisions such as whether to "prioritise feeding their children over themselves", skipping meals and choosing not to heat their homes.

"Food banks are really a lifeline for people in financial crisis," she said.

The rising cost of food has also led to a significant drop in donations over recent years, she added.

"Food banks are having to do more fundraising and to get income to buy food stock so they can pass that on to people."

Sampson-Smith said, as well as providing food parcels and meals, the community pantry also provide a space for people to speak with a cost of living worker and family hub workers.

Appealing for support she said: "We really want to continue. We don't want to stop what we're doing."
